plan: Harder SAT items with near-miss distractors (subtle word choice, two-measure data comparison, evidence time frame), plus S001-03 and S001-06 re-submitted with their labels corrected after blind solvers rated them easier than labelled.

passages.title: Historian
passages.text: Unlike earlier accounts of the mill town's decline, which blamed a single cause, the historian's new study is notably ______: she weighs several possible explanations and openly acknowledges the limits of the surviving records.

passages.title: Tardigrades
passages.text: For years, many biologists assumed that tardigrades, tiny animals that can survive being almost completely dried out, protected themselves mainly by producing a sugar called trehalose, which helps shield cells in some other organisms. Yet when researchers measured trehalose in several tardigrade species, they found little or none. Further work identified proteins found only in tardigrades that form a glass-like gel as the animals dry, apparently protecting their cells until water returns.

passages.title: Highway lanes (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Some transportation planners argue that adding lanes to a congested highway reduces traffic. As evidence, they point to a widening project after which average travel times on the highway fell during the following year.

Text 2
Researchers who study "induced demand" report that when lanes are added to congested highways, travel times often improve at first, but within a few years the new lanes tend to fill as more people choose to drive, and congestion returns to roughly its earlier level.

passages.title: Orchard poem
passages.text: In an original poem titled "The Old Orchard," the speaker describes a neglected orchard as both decaying and still productive, as this line shows: ______

passages.title: Library visits
passages.text:
A researcher compared library visits in three towns.
Town | Visits in 2019 | Visits in 2023
A | 12,000 | 15,000
B | 30,000 | 34,500
C | 8,000 | 10,400
The researcher noted that the town with the largest percentage increase in visits was not the town with the largest increase in the number of visits.

passages.title: Exhibit
passages.text: The museum's new exhibit focuses on three everyday objects whose inventors are largely forgotten ______ the folding ladder, the safety pin, and the paper clip.

passages.title: Volunteers
passages.text: Each of the volunteers who staffed the information booths ______ given a reusable water bottle at the end of the festival.

passages.title: Two scientists
passages.text: Although the two ______ findings at first seemed to contradict each other, a closer look showed that they had measured the lake's temperature at different depths.

passages.title: Park
passages.text: Some critics predicted that the redesigned riverside park would attract few visitors. ______ attendance during its first summer was double that of the previous year.

passages.title: Mural notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Lin Adeyemi was a twentieth-century painter.
• She painted large murals in train stations.
• Her murals depicted ordinary commuters.
• Her 1962 mural Morning Platform is her best-known work.

passages.title: Learning words (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Some teachers argue that the fastest way for students to build vocabulary is to memorize lists of words and their definitions. Students can review dozens of words in a single sitting, and quiz scores often rise within days.

Text 2
Researchers who study reading point out that definitions memorized for a quiz are often forgotten within weeks. Words met repeatedly in meaningful reading, by contrast, tend to be retained, because readers see how the words are actually used.

passages.title: Shell chains
passages.text: Marine biologists have observed that when an empty shell larger than any in a group appears, hermit crabs nearby often line up by size beside it. When the largest crab moves into the new shell, the next crab in line takes the shell it left behind, and so on down the line. This pattern suggests that ______

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: she weighs several possible explanations and openly acknowledges the limits of the surviving records
candidates.explanation: The study weighs several explanations and admits the limits of its evidence, which describes a careful, restrained approach: "measured."

A.rationale: "Strident" means loud and forceful, the opposite of careful weighing.

C.rationale: "Cursory" means hasty and superficial, but the study weighs several explanations.

D.rationale: "Dogmatic" means insisting on one view, but the study considers several and admits uncertainty.

hints: What does the colon tell you about the study's approach?
Which word describes careful, restrained judgment?
candidates.remember: The words after a colon define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents two competing explanations and concludes that neither is supported.
choices.B: It describes an experiment and then lists that experiment's limitations.
choices.C: It describes a long-held assumption, presents evidence against it, and then reports an alternative explanation.
choices.D: It introduces an animal and compares it with other organisms that produce trehalose.

candidates.evidence: Yet when researchers measured trehalose in several tardigrade species, they found little or none.
candidates.explanation: The text opens with an assumption (trehalose protects tardigrades), gives evidence against it (little or no trehalose found), and ends with an alternative (tardigrade-specific proteins forming a gel).

A.rationale: The text does reach a supported explanation: the proteins.

B.rationale: No limitations of an experiment are listed.

D.rationale: The text mentions other organisms only briefly and does not compare tardigrades with them.

hints: Track the text sentence by sentence: assumption, then what?
What does the last sentence offer?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence's role, then match the sequence.

candidates.remember: Structure questions: label each sentence's job.

author_checklist.note: fact note: low or absent trehalose in some tardigrades and tardigrade-specific gel-forming proteins are well documented; stated generically

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely view the evidence cited by the planners in Text 1?

choices.A: As proof that widening a highway immediately increases congestion
choices.B: As evidence that drivers generally prefer narrower roads
choices.C: As fabricated data that should be ignored
choices.D: As likely accurate but covering too short a period to show a lasting effect

candidates.evidence: travel times often improve at first, but within a few years the new lanes tend to fill
candidates.explanation: Text 1's evidence covers only the year after widening. Text 2 agrees that travel times often improve at first but says congestion returns within a few years. So the researchers would accept the evidence but judge it too short-term to support a lasting conclusion.

A.rationale: Text 2 says travel times improve at first, not that congestion rises immediately.

B.rationale: Neither text discusses a preference for narrower roads.

C.rationale: Text 2 does not dispute the data; it disputes what the data show over time.

hints: What time period does Text 1's evidence cover?
What does Text 2 say happens after that period?

strategy.explanation: Compare the time frames of the two texts.

candidates.remember: Short-term evidence may not show long-term effects.

candidates.stem: Which quotation from "The Old Orchard" most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "Wind has stripped the orchard to its bones."
choices.B: "Each autumn the pickers fill their baskets."
choices.D: "The branches sag with rot, and still they bloom."

candidates.evidence: describes a neglected orchard as both decaying and still productive
candidates.explanation: The claim has two parts: decaying and still productive. "The branches sag with rot" shows decay, and "still they bloom" shows continued growth. Only D shows both.

B.rationale: This shows productivity only, and it describes the pickers, not the orchard's condition.

C.rationale: This describes the farmhouse, not the orchard.

hints: The claim has two parts. What are they?
Which quotation shows both at once?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate quotations that show only one half of the claim.

candidates.remember: Two-part claims need evidence for both parts.

author_checklist.note: the poem and its lines are original

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's observation?

choices.A: Town B had more library visits than either other town in both 2019 and 2023.
choices.B: Town C's visits rose by 30 percent, the largest percentage increase, while Town B's visits rose by 4,500, the largest increase in the number of visits.
choices.C: Town A's visits rose from 12,000 to 15,000, an increase of 3,000.
choices.D: All three towns had more library visits in 2023 than in 2019.

candidates.evidence: the town with the largest percentage increase in visits was not the town with the largest increase in the number of visits
candidates.explanation: Increases: A +3,000 (25%), B +4,500 (15%), C +2,400 (30%). Town C has the largest percentage increase, but Town B has the largest increase in number. B states exactly that contrast.

A.rationale: Total visits do not address either kind of increase.

C.rationale: This gives one town's change without the comparison the observation requires.

D.rationale: This is true but does not distinguish percentage increase from numerical increase.

hints: Compute each town's increase in number and as a percent.
Which choice names both leaders?

strategy.explanation: The observation contrasts two measures; find the choice that gives both.

candidates.remember: Percent change and absolute change can rank differently.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the folding ladder, the safety pin, and the paper clip
candidates.explanation: The first part is a complete sentence that announces three objects, and the list that follows names them. A colon correctly introduces a list after a complete clause.

B.rationale: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the list is not a clause.

C.rationale: "Which" cannot introduce a list of nouns without a verb.

D.rationale: "And" joins the list to the clause ungrammatically, leaving no verb for the list.

hints: Is the part before the blank a complete sentence?
What punctuation introduces a list that explains what came before?

strategy.explanation: A complete clause followed by a list calls for a colon.

candidates.remember: Use a colon after a complete clause to introduce a list.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Each of the volunteers who staffed the information booths
candidates.explanation: The subject is "Each," which is singular; "of the volunteers who staffed the information booths" describes it. The singular past-tense verb "was" agrees and matches "at the end of the festival."

A.rationale: "Were" agrees with "volunteers" or "booths," not the true subject "Each."

hints: What is the subject: "each" or "volunteers"?
Is "each" singular or plural?

strategy.explanation: Strip the phrase: "Each … ______ given a bottle."

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: they had measured the lake's temperature at different depths
candidates.explanation: The findings belong to two scientists, so the plural possessive is needed. For a plural noun ending in s, add only an apostrophe: "scientists'."

A.rationale: "Scientist's" is singular possessive, but there are two scientists.

B.rationale: "Scientists" without an apostrophe is a plain plural, not a possessive.

C.rationale: "Scientists's" is not standard for a plural possessive.

hints: How many scientists are there?
How is a plural noun ending in s made possessive?
candidates.remember: Plural possessive: add just an apostrophe after s.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: Some critics predicted that the redesigned riverside park would attract few visitors.
candidates.explanation: The critics predicted few visitors; attendance instead doubled. "On the contrary" signals that the second sentence contradicts the prediction.

A.rationale: "Similarly" signals agreement, but doubled attendance contradicts the prediction.

B.rationale: "Therefore" signals a result, but the prediction did not cause the attendance.

D.rationale: Doubled attendance is not an example of the critics' prediction.

hints: Did the attendance match or contradict the prediction?
Pick the transition for that relationship.
candidates.remember: Name the relationship, then the transition.

candidates.stem: The student wants to introduce Lin Adeyemi and her best-known work to an audience unfamiliar with her. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Lin Adeyemi, a twentieth-century painter known for her murals of ordinary commuters in train stations, is best remembered for her 1962 mural Morning Platform.
choices.B: Morning Platform is Lin Adeyemi's best-known mural.
choices.C: Ordinary commuters appear in many murals painted in train stations.
choices.D: In 1962, a mural called Morning Platform was painted.

candidates.evidence: Her 1962 mural Morning Platform is her best-known work.
candidates.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs to know who Adeyemi was as well as her best-known work. A identifies her as a twentieth-century muralist of commuters and names Morning Platform.

B.rationale: This names the work but does not tell an unfamiliar audience who Adeyemi was.

C.rationale: This does not mention Adeyemi or her work.

hints: What does an audience unfamiliar with her need to know first?
Which choice covers both the painter and the work?

strategy.explanation: The goal has two parts: introduce her and her best-known work.

candidates.remember: Introductions identify the subject before details.

author_checklist.note: Adeyemi and the mural are invented

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?

choices.A: They would argue that quizzes are the most reliable way to measure vocabulary growth.
choices.B: They would grant that memorizing lists can raise quiz scores quickly but question whether those gains last.
choices.C: They would claim that students cannot learn any new words by memorizing lists.
choices.D: They would suggest that reading builds vocabulary faster than memorizing lists does.

candidates.evidence: definitions memorized for a quiz are often forgotten within weeks
candidates.explanation: Text 1 claims lists are the fastest way to build vocabulary, citing quick quiz gains. Text 2 does not deny quick gains; it says memorized definitions are often forgotten within weeks, while words met in reading tend to stick. So the researchers would accept the short-term gains but doubt they last.

A.rationale: Text 2 implies quiz results can mislead, since memorized words fade; it does not call quizzes the most reliable measure.

C.rationale: Text 2 says memorized words are "often forgotten," not that students learn none; "cannot learn any" goes too far.

D.rationale: Text 2 argues that reading leads to better retention, not faster learning.

hints: Does Text 2 deny that lists raise quiz scores?
What does Text 2 say happens weeks later?

strategy.explanation: Find where Text 2 addresses memorized definitions, then pick the response that matches its partial agreement.

candidates.remember: Watch for partial agreement and extreme wording.

revision_history.reason: labelled hard; blind solvers estimated 68-80% correct. Text unchanged, relabelled medium.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: hermit crabs generally prefer shells that are too small for them.
choices.B: only the largest crab in the group ends up with a better-fitting shell.
choices.C: hermit crabs line up beside a new shell without regard to their size.
choices.D: a single new shell can lead to several crabs in the group moving into larger shells.

candidates.evidence: When the largest crab moves into the new shell, the next crab in line takes the shell it left behind, and so on down the line.
candidates.explanation: Each crab that moves leaves its old shell for the next crab, and the chain continues down the line. So one new shell lets many crabs upgrade, not just one.

A.rationale: The crabs move into larger shells, which suggests they seek a better fit, not smaller shells.

B.rationale: The chain of moves means crabs after the largest one also get larger shells.

C.rationale: The text says the crabs line up by size.

hints: Follow the chain: what happens to each shell that is left behind?
How many crabs end up in a new shell?

strategy.explanation: Trace the sequence in the second sentence to its result.

candidates.remember: Completion questions follow the text's logic to its next step.

author_checklist.fact_note: shell vacancy chains in hermit crabs are a well-documented behavior; no researcher is named
